subject: Historia
title: Prehistory and the first civilisations
sourceSummary: The Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age, how farming changed human life, the first civilisations in Mesopotamia and Egypt, the importance of writing, and how historians use sources and remains.
topics: the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age

questions.topic: the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age
questions.prompt: Why is the oldest period in human history called the Stone Age?
questions.opener: The periods are named after the material the tools were made from.
choices: People lived exclusively in caves made of stone
There was only stone and nothing else on Earth
Tools and weapons were mainly made of stone, wood and bone
The first stone houses were built during this time
questions.explanation: The name comes from people making their most important tools from stone, for example axes, knives and spearheads made of flint. Not everyone lived in caves — huts and tents of hide and wood were also built — the name is about the material of the tools, not the dwellings.

questions.prompt: What was an important consequence of people starting to farm crops and keep animals instead of hunting and gathering?
questions.opener: Think about how often you need to move if food grows in one and the same place.
choices: People could settle in the same place and villages grew up
People began wandering even further each year
The population fell because food ran out
People stopped using tools altogether
questions.explanation: With farming, food was available in the same place year after year, so people could become settled and build villages. Hunters and gatherers instead needed to move following game and the seasons — so it was the nomadic way of life that declined, not the settled one.

questions.prompt: Between which two rivers did Mesopotamia, one of the world's first areas of civilisation, lie?
questions.opener: The name Mesopotamia roughly means "the land between the rivers".
choices: The Nile and the Congo River
The Euphrates and the Tigris
The Danube and the Rhine
The Ganges and the Indus
questions.explanation: Mesopotamia lay between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris, in the area that today is mostly Iraq. There, the rivers' water made the soil fertile enough to support large cities. The Nile instead belongs to Egypt, and the Indus to another early civilisation in present-day Pakistan.

questions.prompt: Why was the Nile so important for ancient Egypt?
questions.opener: Think about what the river left behind on the fields every year.
choices: It provided protection against all enemies
It meant the Egyptians didn't need to grow food
It was cold and cooled the country down
Its annual floods made the soil fertile and gave water to the crops
questions.explanation: The Nile flooded every year and laid down a layer of nutrient-rich silt on the fields, giving good harvests in an otherwise very dry country. So the Egyptians were in fact able to farm largely thanks to the river — it was the country's lifeline for food, drinking water and transport alike.

questions.prompt: What was the most important significance of the invention of writing?
questions.opener: Think about what you can do with information once it doesn't only exist in memory.
choices: All people learned to read at once
People could stop using spoken language
Knowledge, laws and business could be recorded and passed on over time
People could start building houses out of stone
questions.explanation: With writing, you could record how much grain had been handed in, what laws applied and what had happened — the information was preserved and could be read much later. Only a small few, often scribes and priests, could read and write to begin with, though, so it wasn't everyone who learned.

questions.prompt: How do historians and archaeologists gain knowledge about the time before people began writing?
questions.opener: If there are no texts — what is left in the ground to examine?
choices: By reading diaries from the Stone Age
By examining remains such as tools, graves, bone fragments and settlements
By guessing based on how we live today
By interviewing people who remember
questions.explanation: The time before writing is called prehistoric precisely because written sources are missing. Knowledge instead comes from the material remains that archaeologists dig up: tools, pottery shards, graves, bones and traces of settlements. Diaries didn't exist, and no living person can remember that far back.

questions.prompt: Explain step by step how farming could lead to the first cities growing up.
questions.opener: Start with the food: what happens when you can grow more than you need yourself?
questions.answer: When people learned to grow grain and keep livestock, they could produce more food than they themselves needed. The surplus meant that some people could take up activities other than food production, such as crafts, trade, religion or governing. More people could live closely together in the same place, villages grew into cities, and cities needed rules, leaders and a way of keeping track of stores — which, among other things, led to writing.
steps: Farming made people settled: food remained available in the same place year after year.
Good harvests gave a food surplus that could be stored.
Not everyone needed to farm any more, so some could become craftspeople, priests, soldiers or merchants.
More people could be supported on a small area, and villages grew into cities with thousands of inhabitants.
Cities required leaders, laws and record-keeping of the stores, which contributed to the invention of writing.

questions.topic: the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age
questions.prompt: Summarise the periods of prehistory and the first civilisations.
questions.opener: Go through the three ages in order, then the first civilisations and the sources.
questions.answer: The Stone Age: the longest period, tools of stone, wood and bone · first hunters and gatherers, later farmers as agriculture spread · The Bronze Age (in Sweden about 1800-500 BC): bronze is a mixture of copper and tin, harder than stone, but the metal had to be traded over long distances · The Iron Age (in Sweden about 500 BC-1050 AD): iron was found in more places, became cheaper and gave better tools and weapons · The agricultural revolution: settled life, food surplus, more occupations, villages growing into cities · Mesopotamia: between the Euphrates and the Tigris, the Sumerians, cuneiform writing, one of the world's first civilisations · Egypt: around the Nile, annual floods gave fertile soil, hieroglyphs, pharaohs and pyramids · The importance of writing: knowledge, laws and business could be preserved and passed on · Historical sources: written sources only exist after the invention of writing, before that knowledge is built on archaeological remains such as tools, graves and settlements.

questions.topic: the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age
questions.prompt: What characterised the Bronze Age compared with the Stone Age?
questions.opener: Bronze is a metal that has to be made by mixing two other metals.
choices: Tools were made from a mixture of copper and tin, which was harder than stone
People stopped hunting entirely
It was the first period with farming
Metals weren't used at all
questions.explanation: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin and gave harder, sharper tools and weapons than stone. Farming had already begun in the later Stone Age, and hunting still continued alongside farming.

questions.prompt: Where in the world did farming first arise, according to archaeological finds?
questions.opener: The area is sometimes called the Fertile Crescent and lies in today's Middle East.
choices: In northern Europe
In the Middle East, in the so-called Fertile Crescent
In South America
In Australia
questions.explanation: The oldest traces of farming are found in the Middle East, in the Fertile Crescent around the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, about 10,000-12,000 years ago. Farming later arose independently elsewhere in the world too, but the Middle East is counted among the very earliest.

questions.prompt: What was typical of the early civilisations in Mesopotamia and Egypt?
questions.opener: Think about what distinguishes a civilisation from smaller, scattered villages.
choices: They had no cities at all
They had cities, writing, a ruling elite and organised farming around rivers
They lived entirely as hunters and gatherers
They had no contact with each other at all
questions.explanation: Both Mesopotamia and Egypt had large cities, developed writing, a ruling upper class and organised farming that made use of the rivers' water. There was also trade and contact between the different early civilisations.

questions.prompt: What writing system was developed in Mesopotamia?
questions.opener: The signs were pressed into clay tablets with a wedge-shaped stylus.
choices: Hieroglyphs
Cuneiform
The Latin alphabet
Runes
questions.explanation: The Sumerians in Mesopotamia developed cuneiform writing, where signs were pressed into clay tablets. Hieroglyphs instead belonged to ancient Egypt, and runes were used much later in the Nordic region.

questions.prompt: What is the period before writing was invented called?
questions.opener: The name describes the fact that written sources are entirely absent from this period.
choices: Antiquity
The Middle Ages
Prehistoric times
The Early Modern era
questions.explanation: Prehistoric times is the name for the period before writing was invented, when knowledge is built on archaeological remains rather than texts. Antiquity, the Middle Ages and the Early Modern era all come after writing was already in use in several places.

questions.topic: the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age
questions.prompt: Explain step by step why the Iron Age was a major advance compared with the Bronze Age.
questions.opener: Think about where copper, tin and iron are found in nature, and what that means for the price of the metal.
questions.answer: Iron was available in more places in nature than the copper and tin that bronze requires, so people didn't need to trade over such long distances to get hold of the metal. This made iron cheaper and more accessible to more people, leading to better and sharper tools and weapons for a larger share of the population, not just the wealthy who had previously been able to afford imported bronze.
steps: Bronze requires both copper and tin, and tin was only found in a few places in Europe, so the metal had to be traded over long distances and became expensive.
Iron ore, on the other hand, was found in considerably more places, often close to where people already lived.
Since iron was easier to get hold of, it became cheaper to make tools and weapons out of iron.
More people, not just the wealthiest, therefore gained access to better equipment for farming, hunting and war.
The result was sharper axes, ploughs and weapons that spread to far more people in society than during the Bronze Age.

questions.prompt: Which writing system did ancient Egypt use?
questions.opener: The signs are often pictures of animals, people and objects.
choices: Cuneiform
Hieroglyphs
Runes
The Greek alphabet
questions.explanation: Ancient Egypt used hieroglyphs, a writing system of pictorial signs. Cuneiform instead belonged to Mesopotamia, and runes and the Greek alphabet arose in entirely different places much later.
